strengths: The paper addresses a practically important problem in text-to-audio generation: reducing the high inference latency of diffusion- and flow-based TTA systems.

The method is technically coherent: it adapts the MeanFlow average-velocity objective to latent audio generation, integrates classifier-free guidance into training to avoid an extra inference branch, and introduces an instantaneous-to-mean curriculum that stabilizes learning of the JVP-based target.

The AudioCaps results are strong and practically relevant. MeanAudio uses only a 120M backbone, achieves one-step generation with RTF 0.013, and attains the best reported one-step FAD, FD, KL, IS, and CLAP scores among the accelerated models; its 2-, 5-, and 25-step results are also competitive with much larger multi-step systems.

The ablations on training initialization, flow mix-up ratio, and CFG scale provide useful empirical evidence for the proposed training strategy and show why direct mean-flow training from scratch is unstable.
The lightweight model and relatively low GPU training cost make the approach attractive for deployment, and the stated intention to release code and weights could support follow-up work.
weaknesses: Conceptual novelty is limited. The core MeanFlow objective, mixed-flow training, and guidance-distillation idea are taken from prior work, while the Flux/MMDiT-style architecture combines existing components. The main contribution is therefore an application and engineering adaptation rather than a substantial new generative-modeling principle.

The evaluation is too narrow for the breadth of the 'state-of-the-art' and 'faithful' claims. Results are reported only on AudioCaps, with no Clotho or out-of-domain evaluation, no human quality/text-alignment study, no preference test, and little qualitative failure analysis. FAD, FD, IS, and CLAP are useful proxies but do not fully establish perceptual fidelity or prompt faithfulness.

The speed comparison requires more transparency. It is unclear whether RTF includes FLAN-T5/CLAP encoding, VAE decoding, and vocoding, as well as batch size, precision, warm-up, and caching. The 100x figure is specifically relative to GenAU/200 NFEs; against TangoFlux/50 steps the wall-clock gain is much smaller. Several recently discussed accelerated systems are also absent from the main comparison.

There are several reproducibility gaps. The code and project links are placeholders, and the paper does not fully specify the audio sampling rate, pretrained VAE/vocoder checkpoints, multi-step timestep schedules, random seeds, or how the conditional and instantaneous-to-mean curriculum are implemented in detail.

Algorithm 1 and the integrated-CFG formulation need clarification. The target requires conditional and unconditional predictions at r=t, but the algorithm does not explain how these are obtained, whether extra forward passes are used, or how the JVP is conditioned. The stated effective guidance scale ω/(1−κ) is not directly derived from the displayed weighted combination.

The experimental reporting lacks confidence intervals, multiple training seeds, or sensitivity analysis for caption selection and generation randomness. With only one benchmark and one main run, the robustness of the metric improvements is difficult to judge.

Architectural modifications such as ConvMLP, RoPE, RMSNorm, and the mixture of multi-modal and audio-only blocks are not independently ablated, so their contribution to the reported performance is unsupported.

strengths: The paper addresses an important practical bottleneck in text-to-audio generation. The reported one-step model is compact (120M parameters) and achieves RTF 0.013 on an RTX 3090, compared with RTF 1.612 for the 200-step GenAU system, giving a roughly 100x latency reduction for the main open-source diffusion baseline.

The core Mean Flow adaptation is technically coherent: regressing the average velocity over a flow interval enables direct mapping from noise to audio latent, while the instantaneous-to-mean curriculum and flow mix-up are reasonable ways to stabilize training.
Integrating classifier-free guidance into the training target is a useful design because it can preserve guidance at inference without doubling the number of model evaluations.

The empirical study is broad for a systems paper: it evaluates AudioCaps and MusicCaps, several NFE settings, objective and human metrics, data/model scaling, and ablations over the curriculum, flow-mix ratio, architectural components, and guidance scale.

Training resource requirements and hyperparameters are reported in useful detail, including GPU type, iteration counts, learning-rate schedules, batch sizes, and total training time. The commitment to release code and weights would further support follow-up research.
weaknesses: The technical contribution is primarily an application and combination of existing methods—Mean Flow, Flux-style transformers, MMDiT, dual CLAP/T5 conditioning, and known architectural refinements—rather than a substantial new generative modeling or NLP method. This makes it more naturally a Findings contribution than a strong main-conference paper.

The classifier-free guidance presentation is internally inconsistent. Equation (3) assigns κ to the conditional prediction and 1−ω−κ to the unconditional prediction, whereas Algorithm 1 reverses these terms. The claimed effective guidance scale ω/(1−κ)=3 is also not derived from the stated coefficients, so the exact implemented formula is ambiguous.

Algorithm 2 is insufficiently precise about the inference timestep ordering and signs. The training convention has data at t=0 and noise at t=1, but the update formula and unspecified t_i schedule can appear sign-reversed; the argument order for r and t is also used inconsistently. This could materially hinder independent reproduction.

The claim that the curriculum accelerates convergence is not directly tested. The paper reports final quality but provides no loss curves, time-to-threshold comparisons, or accounting for the cost of full-dataset pretraining, so faster convergence remains an assertion rather than evidence.

The human evaluation is small and under-specified. It uses ten audio experts, but the number of ratings per model, prompt balancing, blinding procedure, inter-rater agreement, and statistical significance of the reported differences are not clear; the dual-encoder study uses only three listeners.

Reproducibility is not yet fully supported in the manuscript: the Code and Demo fields are blank, and important implementation details such as the FLAN-T5 version, exact VAE/vocoder checkpoints, inference schedule, random seeds, and multiple-run variance are missing.

Some SOTA and speed claims are broader than the evidence strictly supports. The one-step model is strongest among accelerated one-step systems, but it does not dominate all multi-step systems on every metric, and the 100x comparison is specifically to selected diffusion baselines rather than every existing TTA system.

Data provenance needs clarification. In particular, training includes LP-MusicCaps-MC while MusicCaps is used for evaluation, so explicit exclusion of the MusicCaps test items and any duplicate audio should be documented. The dataset table also does not align cleanly with the stated WavCaps source composition.
